blocks.text: 但我们经常看到企业为每个团队或问题类型分配自己的子代理，代理架构变成了其组织架构图的翻版（康威定律在起作用）。

blocks.text: 大型组织的代理构建失败模式

inlines.text: 大型组织的代理构建失败模式

blocks.text: 公司通常希望构建一个代理，将多个产品和能力统一到一个客户界面中。

inlines.text: 公司通常希望构建一个代理，将多个产品和能力统一到一个客户界面中。

blocks.text: 通常，每项能力由不同的团队负责，因此公司一开始让每个团队构建自己的代理，然后由一个中央平台团队在其上构建编排器。这可以采取多种结构，包括编排器-子代理，或将特定代理作为 MCP 工具暴露的单一代理。

inlines.text: 通常，每项能力由不同的团队负责，因此公司一开始让每个团队构建自己的代理，然后由一个中央平台团队在其上构建编排器。这可以采取多种结构，包括编排器-子代理，或将特定代理作为 MCP 工具暴露的单一代理。

blocks.text: 这看起来是最简单的解决方案，但会立即引入以下复杂性：

inlines.text: 这看起来是最简单的解决方案，但会立即引入以下复杂性：
上下文管理：
你需要决定代理之间交换哪些上下文，并且经常在来回传递中丢失细节。
子代理泛滥
：每个团队都发布自己的子代理，因此公司最终会有数百个重叠的子代理，没有强制执行的标准，也没有明确的负责人。
拼凑式提示词
：每个团队都往系统提示词里加一句话，导致规则相互冲突、语气前后不一。
未经审核、过度本地化的评估
：每个人都添加自己的评估，且过度针对自己的子任务进行优化。没有人负责或维护整套评估，而管理层依据被稀释、过度本地化的分数做决策。
延迟
：多智能体架构的复杂性会增加延迟。一位客户将其多智能体框架与单智能体循环进行对比评估，发现后者的运行速度约快 2 倍。

blocks.text: 使用带渐进式披露的智能体循环

inlines.text: 使用带渐进式披露的智能体循环

blocks.text: 上述编排器-子智能体设计是协调跨团队构建的专家智能体的一种合理方式，但通常更有效的方法是通过技能渐进式披露上下文以及通过工具搜索渐进式披露工具。换言之，智能体只看到技能和工具的简短描述，仅在需要时才完整加载。

inlines.text: 上述编排器-子智能体设计是协调跨团队构建的专家智能体的一种合理方式，但通常更有效的方法是
通过技能渐进式披露上下文
以及
通过工具搜索渐进式披露工具
。换言之，智能体只看到技能和工具的简短描述，仅在需要时才完整加载。

blocks.text: 这种方法之所以合理，有三个原因：

inlines.text: 这种方法之所以合理，有三个原因：
共享上下文能产生更好的答案：
对于长时间运行的智能体，我们希望来自多个不同任务的上下文都留在主上下文窗口中。一个已经看到每个先前步骤结果的智能体可以将它们联系起来，从而产生比子智能体交回的一组摘要更丰富的输出和更好的洞察。这也意味着
更少的上下文窗口和更少的有损交接
渐进式披露可防止上下文膨胀：
这项技术
让团队能够构建单个智能体来完成各种各样的任务，而无需将所有上下文立即加载到一个冗长的系统提示词中。这消除了团队此前将工作拆分给子智能体的主要原因。事实上，我们
将 Claude Code 面向更高级模型的系统提示词缩减了 80% 以上
，其中就包括与渐进式披露技能和工具相关的删减。
模型能力更强：
从 Opus 4.5 开始，模型在单个循环中能处理的事情远超大多数团队的预期。你无法关闭 Opus 5.5 的思考功能，而 Fable 5.1 以及近期模型越来越多地会叙述自己的进展并随时检查工作，这使得某些框架元素变得多余。每一个新模型都让你能把更多决策从框架转移到模型本身。更简单的循环也更容易迁移到下一个模型；在我们帮助客户进行的迁移中，僵化的多智能体结构往往是阻碍新模型承担更多工作的原因。

blocks.text: 单智能体循环设计要求严格自律：精心管理的系统提示词、能在恰当时机触发的技能和工具描述，以及对上下文窗口、记忆和笔记的审慎处理。本文后续章节将深入探讨迁移和设计方面的考量。

blocks.text: 如何将子智能体并入主智能体循环

inlines.text: 如何将子智能体并入主智能体循环

blocks.text: 许多团队已经在生产环境中拥有一个编排器和一组专家智能体。以下是我们建议逐步采用的一种单一循环设计：

inlines.text: 许多团队已经在生产环境中拥有一个编排器和一组专家智能体。以下是我们建议逐步采用的一种单一循环设计：
一个模型和一个上下文窗口运行开放式工具循环，并在 harness 中设置限制（轮次和成本预算、写入闸门）。
每一轮，模型发出一批工具调用。harness 并行运行它们，并将原始结果返回给同一个模型，由它决定下一步：再发一批、向用户提问，还是给出答案。
当模型给出答案或触及
预算
时，循环停止。可选地在答案之后运行目标或验证器检查。
模型在第一轮将计划写入上下文，并随着结果到达而修订计划。这是与编排器和专家智能体设置的主要区别：编写计划的模型也是执行计划的模型，因此它可以在轮次中途更改计划。
Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:
不再需要从规则目录重写计划的代码步骤，因为模型会决定每一步。
排序和领域流程移入
技能。
硬性限制（验证、审批闸门）以及对话中途出现的任何其他内容（例如记忆查找）移入
工具。
代码仍可用于加载任何廉价且几乎总是相关的内容（例如实体解析步骤），并用于处理循环所调用工具内部的任何机械部分（载荷构建、流解析、恢复澄清）。

blocks.text: 这种单一循环设计也有助于实现许多团队正在努力达成的最终状态（一个理解用户高层目标并代表用户行动的智能体），因为它将智能体学到的一切都保留在一个上下文中。

blocks.text: 任务完成度评估

inlines.text: 任务完成度评估

blocks.text: 第一步是创建一个评估集，帮助你判断是否应将某个子智能体并入主智能体循环。我们见过的有效评估结构是：一个由中央团队拥有的共享端到端评估集，以及由各技能所属团队随每个技能发布的小型评估集。即使只有 10 个黄金示例也足以开始。

inlines.text: 第一步是创建一个评估集，帮助你判断是否应将某个子智能体并入主智能体循环。我们见过的有效评估结构是：一个由中央团队拥有的共享端到端评估集，以及由各技能所属团队随每个技能发布的小型评估集。即使只有 10 个黄金示例也足以开始。

blocks.text: 根据评分标准对智能体的最终消息进行评分，是跟踪答案质量的良好起点。当你仍拥有编排器时，还应跟踪路由准确性（它是否选择了正确的子智能体？）。一旦子智能体被并入，就改为检查智能体是否加载了正确的技能或调用了正确的工具。逐步推进任务完成度评估是有益的，因为在比较架构时这一点最为重要。

inlines.text: 将子代理作为工具调用

blocks.text: 当上述三个条件之一适用且你保留某个子代理时，让主代理将子代理作为工具调用会很有效，这样主代理可以继续与用户保持对话。

inlines.text: 当上述三个条件之一适用且你保留某个子代理时，让主代理将子代理作为工具调用会很有效，这样主代理可以继续与用户保持对话。

blocks.text: 我们只建议在子代理需要直接与用户交谈时，才进行完全交接，即由子代理接管对话。其他一切都可以作为主循环中的技能加工具。

blocks.text: 当智能体需要执行操作、从系统读取实时数据，或以固定格式返回结果时，工具是合适的选择。你也可以把工具当作在迁移期间继续调用子智能体的一种方式。我们建议按用户意图对工具进行分组（而不是每个 API 一个工具），因为一旦系统提示中的工具定义超过 30-50 个，工具选择往往会退化。

blocks.text: Agent building failure modes for large organizations

inlines.text: Agent building failure modes for large organizations

blocks.text: Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.

inlines.text: Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.

blocks.text: Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.

inlines.text: Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.

blocks.text: This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:

inlines.text: This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:
Context management:
You need to decide what context is exchanged between agents and often lose details in the back and forth.
Subagent sprawl
: Every team ships its own subagent, so companies end up with hundreds of overlapping subagents with no enforced standards and no specific owner.
The Frankenprompt
: Every team adds a sentence to the system prompt, resulting in conflicting rules and no consistent voice.
Unvetted, overly localized evals
: Everyone adds their own evals that are overly optimized for their subtask. No one owns or maintains the whole set, and leadership makes decisions based on watered-down, overly localized scores.
Latency
: Multi-agent architectural complexity adds latency. One customer that evaluated their multi-agent harness against a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter.

blocks.text: Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure

inlines.text: Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure

blocks.text: The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be progressively disclosing context via skills and progressively disclosing tools via tool search. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.

inlines.text: The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be
progressively disclosing context via skills
and
progressively disclosing tools via tool search
. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.

blocks.text: There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:

inlines.text: There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:
Shared context produces better answers:

for longer-running agents, we want the context from several different tasks to sit in the main context window. An agent that has seen the result of each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs and better insights than a set of summaries handed back by subagents. It also means
fewer context windows and fewer lossy handoffs
Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat:
this technique

allows teams to build single agents that can accomplish a wide variety of tasks without requiring all of the context to be immediately loaded into one long system prompt. This removes the main reason teams previously split work across subagents. In fact, we
reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80%
which included cuts related to progressively disclosing skills and tools.
Models are more capable:

starting with Opus 4.5, models became capable of managing far more in a single loop than most teams expected. You cannot turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, and recent models increasingly narrate their progress and check their work as they go, which makes some harness elements redundant. Each new model lets you move more of the decision-making out of the harness and into the model itself. A simpler loop is also easier to move to the next model; in migrations we have helped customers with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work.

blocks.text: The single agent loop design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context windows, memory, and note-taking. This article goes deeper into migration and design considerations in subsequent sections.

blocks.text: One central team should own end-to-end quality and the system prompt, vetting every new tool and eval before it ships. Keeping that central team small helps iteration move quickly and lowers coordination cost across a large org.

blocks.text: If you go the multi-agent route, start with the simplest pattern (generator-verifier, orchestrator-subagent, or other) that could work. Decompose boundaries effectively by dividing by context: give each subagent a piece of work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result (good candidates are independent research paths, separate components with clean interfaces, or black-box verification). When agents are split by problem type, they engage in a "telephone game," passing information back and forth with each handoff degrading fidelity.

blocks.text: How to fold subagents into the main agent loop

inlines.text: How to fold subagents into the main agent loop

blocks.text: Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:

inlines.text: Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:
One model and one context window running an open-ended tool loop, with limits (turn and cost budgets, write gates) set in the harness.

Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls. The harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step: another batch, a question to the user, or an answer.
The loop stops when the model answers or hits a
budget
. A goal or verifier check can optionally run after the answer.

The model writes its plan in context on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change from the orchestrator and specialist agents setup: the model that writes the plan is also the one carrying it out, so it can change the plan mid-turn.
Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:
A code step that rewrites the plan from a catalog of rules is no longer needed, since the model decides each step.
Ordering and domain procedure move into
skills.
Hard limits (validation, approval gates) and anything else that comes up mid-conversation (e.g. memory lookup) move into the
tools.

Code can still be used to load anything cheap and almost always relevant (e.g. an entity resolution step), and to handle any mechanical parts (payload construction, stream parsing, resuming a clarification) inside tools the loop calls.

blocks.text: This single loop design also helps with the end state many teams are working toward (an agent that understands a user's high-level goals and acts on their behalf), since it keeps everything the agent has learned in one context.

Even a set of 10 golden examples is enough to start.

Working toward task-completion evals over time is helpful as this matters most when comparing architectures.

blocks.text: Merge specialists that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or are often called together. For example, if a significant share of production traffic is one specialist followed by a second, that is a tightly coupled pair, which makes it a candidate to merge into one domain agent.

blocks.text: Folding subagents into the main agent via skills and tools

inlines.text: Folding subagents into the main agent via skills and tools

blocks.text: Fold subagents into the main agent one at a time by turning each one’s prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools. Compare eval performance with and without the subagent. Then decide which to keep.

inlines.text: Fold subagents into the main agent one at a time by turning each one’s prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools. Compare eval performance with and without the subagent. Then decide which to keep.

blocks.text: When you compare, don’t just examine the final score, take a look at which tasks flipped. When we tested this on a sample support agent, folding one subagent into another lowered latency, but also broke a process that had been passing. The main agent was holding the order lookup tool and answering on its own, without asking the shipping specialist for the delivery date.

blocks.text: How several teams can contribute to a single agent

inlines.text: How several teams can contribute to a single agent

blocks.text: Domain reasoning can be retrieved from knowledge bases, skills, and MCP tools. Individual teams can shift their ownership from agents to skills and tools, with one small central team keeping ownership of the system prompt and end-to-end quality. This involves vetting new skills, tools, and evals before they ship.

blocks.text: MCP tools

inlines.text: MCP tools

blocks.text: Tools are the right fit when the agent needs to take an action, read live data from a system, or return a result in a fixed shape. You can also use tools as a way to keep calling subagents while you migrate. We recommend tools grouped by user intent (not one tool per API) because once you exceed 30-50 tool definitions in the system prompt, tool choice tends to degrade.

inlines.text: Tools are the right fit when the agent needs to take an action, read live data from a system, or return a result in a fixed shape. You can also use tools as a way to keep calling subagents while you migrate. We recommend tools grouped by user intent (not one tool per API) because once you exceed 30-50 tool definitions in the system prompt, tool choice tends to degrade.

blocks.text: Use tool search with deferred loading, limit hard preconditions, and move any needed ones into the tools. For example, if Y needs X's output, Y's tool checks for it and returns an instruction the model can act on. Per-user permissions work the same way. Each tool checks what the calling user may see or do and returns a plain refusal the model can read, so one loop can serve users with different access without a separate agent per permission level.

blocks.text: Skills

inlines.text: Skills

blocks.text: Skills are the right fit when the agent needs to know how a team does work, like the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist subagent's prompt used to hold.

inlines.text: Skills are the right fit when the agent needs to know how a team does work, like the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist subagent's prompt used to hold.

blocks.text: Our approach to growing skill libraries is to give the maintenance work back to the people writing the skills. Claude can do the heavy lifting with skills that can build, test, and prune other skills.

blocks.text: To prevent skill sprawl, you can have DRIs per team own their skills and make sure they are well crafted, distinct, and shipped with appropriate evals.

/skill-creator
allows you to author new skills that start well-formed, and audit existing ones to trim, deduplicate, and restructure them.
/skill-doctor
allows you to see what each skill in your library costs and how often it’s actually used, and delete dead weight.

blocks.text: Knowledge bases

inlines.text: Knowledge bases

blocks.text: Knowledge bases are the right fit for reference material the agent only needs some of the time. Facts and reference material (policies, metric definitions, product specs) can sit behind a search or lookup tool the model calls, or ship as reference files inside a skill. Avoid having code retrieve and paste this context into prompts.

blocks.text: Tools to accelerate this work

inlines.text: Tools to accelerate this work

blocks.text: We recently released a set of Claude API skills that can help with most of the work mentioned above. Our migration kit chains these skills together in one guided workflow for assessing and moving multi-agent systems to a single agent loop. It includes a demo you can try before running it on the real thing:

inlines.text: We recently
released
a set of Claude API skills that can help with most of the work mentioned above. Our
migration kit
chains these skills together in one guided workflow for assessing and moving multi-agent systems to a single agent loop. It includes a demo you can try before running it on the real thing:
/claude-api build-eval:
can help create a first end-to-end set owned by the central team or small evals each team ships with its skill
/claude-api prompt-audit:

can flag instructions written for older models in your prompts, skills, and tool descriptions and propose fixes as a diff. This can be run on your system prompts to find any rules that were added for an earlier model and are now making the agent slower or more rigid. Each team's DRI can also run it on their own skills and tool descriptions.
/claude-api hillclimb:

can iteratively improve an app against an existing eval. This can be used for the "folded in vs kept" comparison (after folding one subagent into a skill plus tools, let it iterate on the skill and tool descriptions and see if the folded version matches or beats the subagent), as well as your system prompt.
/claude-api cost-optimize:

profiles where your calls go and proposes savings from options such as prompt caching, trimming unneeded input and output tokens, effort, and model choice, one change at a time. This can help bring cost and latency down on a given design.

blocks.text: As models evolve, our understanding of how to best use them and guidance around best practice evolve as well. That makes any one architecture less important than the principle behind it: measure, change one thing at a time, and keep what holds up.

You don’t have to make that move in one step, though. Build a small end-to-end eval, fold in one subagent, and keep it as a subagent only if the folded version scores worse, then rinse and repeat.
